scenario: A wing exercise ends with leadership directing that a contractor-run 'innovation cell' be stood up within 90 days. The PM has a vendor in mind ('they briefed us at the symposium'), no requirements document, and asks you to 'start the contract paperwork while we figure out the details.'
baits: The 90-day directive implies urgency that hasn't been tested
'Vendor in mind' before any requirement exists
key_moves: No paperwork starts before a requirement definition — push for the need, outcomes, and an IGCE
Symposium familiarity is not market research — run a real capability look
Directed timelines don't create a competition exception; plan backward from 90 days with the real process
follow_ups: What belongs in the requirements conversation?
When would urgency legitimately shortcut competition?

scenario: A services contract's final option year ends in 10 months. The program office says the follow-on 'will just be the same thing again' and asks you to hold off on strategy work until the new PM arrives in the spring — roughly 5 months out.
baits: 'Same thing again' minimizes the strategy work needed
Waiting for the new PM feels reasonable but burns the runway
key_moves: Start now — fresh market research, set-aside look, and requirement scrub take months
A bridge caused by waiting for personnel is a planning failure, not an unforeseen cause
Document the timeline so the record shows deliberate planning
follow_ups: What makes a bridge justification valid?
What could have changed since last award that invalidates 'the same thing'?

scenario: A deployed civil engineer emails a portable-generator vendor 'we accept your quote, ship ASAP' to beat a storm window. The units arrive and work perfectly. The vendor invoices $65K. The engineer says exigency justified it and points out the base commander verbally concurred at the time.
baits: Genuine urgency and a good outcome make it feel excusable
Commander concurrence sounds like authority
key_moves: Neither engineers nor commanders hold contracting authority — this is an unauthorized commitment regardless of outcome
Government benefited and price may be fair → ratification package: statement, fund availability at the time, Legal
$65K ≤ SAT → COCO-level ratification; then train the unit on the emergency-buy channels that DO exist
follow_ups: Which ratification element most often fails?
What lawful rapid-buy tools existed for the storm?

scenario: Reviewing invoices, you find a contractor billing 15% over the award for 'verbal expansions approved by the site lead' across six months — small additions each time, all documented in the contractor's notes but never in a mod. The site lead says 'that's how we've always flexed the work.'
baits: 'How we've always done it' normalizes the violation
Small increments hide the cumulative problem
key_moves: Site leads don't direct work — stop the practice in writing immediately
Sort what happened: unauthorized new work (ratification lane) vs. Government-directed changes to existing work (constructive change/REA lane)
Fix the channel: all direction through the PCO, and brief both the site and the contractor
follow_ups: How do you distinguish ratification from constructive change here?
What does the cumulative 15% do to your scope analysis?

scenario: During proposal evaluations, an SSEB member's spouse posts on LinkedIn congratulating her company — one of the offerors — on 'great momentum on the base network bid.' The evaluator swears he's never discussed the source selection at home and offers to keep evaluating 'since nothing actually leaked.'
baits: 'Nothing actually leaked' — unproven and not his call
The post may be innocent, making inaction feel safe
key_moves: Report to Legal now — the question is what protected information was accessible and whether any moved
The evaluator's continued participation is a decision for the PCO/SSA with Legal, not a self-assessment
Document the facts and the determination whichever way it lands
follow_ups: What's protected under 3.104?
When does an appearance problem become a disqualification problem?

scenario: A week before award, an offeror's VP calls your COCO: 'We heard we're rated second on past performance — we'd like to submit supplemental references.' Nobody outside the team should know any ratings. The COCO wants to 'just decline the references and move on quietly.'
baits: Declining the references feels like it contains the problem
'Move on quietly' avoids schedule pain
key_moves: The call itself is evidence protected information leaked TO an offeror — the serious branch of PIA
Legal immediately; trace the leak; written impact determination — quiet handling creates the protest AND the scandal
Decline the references in writing as an improper exchange, but that's the smallest part of the response
follow_ups: Who decides whether the procurement proceeds?
What are the offeror's obligations when it receives protected info?

scenario: Your engineering-support contractor is helping the program office draft test criteria for an upcoming production competition. You learn the contractor's parent company just acquired one of the likely production bidders. The contractor proposes a firewall memo: separate teams, separate buildings, no shared drives.
baits: The firewall sounds robust and proactive
The acquisition just happened — 'nothing improper occurred yet'
key_moves: Test criteria authorship for a competition your affiliate will enter = biased ground rules — the hardest OCI to mitigate
Firewalls address information flow, not ground rules already being shaped — likely remedy is removing the contractor from the criteria work or excluding the affiliate
PCO decides, Legal advises, before the solicitation moves
follow_ups: Why don't firewalls fix biased ground rules?
What would a valid path look like if the Government wants the affiliate to compete?

scenario: On your A&AS multiple-award IDIQ, Holder A's analysts maintain the program's requirements database. A new task order competition opens to all five holders — and Holder A's proposal cites specific unfunded requirements from that database as 'anticipated growth' no other holder mentions.
baits: Holder A did nothing overtly wrong — they used what they knew
The insight makes their proposal genuinely better
key_moves: Unequal access to non-public information — no bad act required; the imbalance is the conflict
Options: neutralize (share the same data with all holders and allow revisions) or address Holder A's access in the evaluation, with Legal
Fix the structure: database-support roles need OCI clauses and data walls before the next competition
follow_ups: Can you cure this mid-competition? How?
What contract language prevents this on support task orders?

scenario: Your apparent awardee on a $700K paving contract lists an office address that turns out to be a mailbox store, has no equipment in its own name ('we lease everything per job'), and its listed superintendent also appears full-time on another company's website. Price is excellent and references check out by phone.
baits: Good references and price pull toward award
Leasing equipment is legitimately common in construction
key_moves: Run the standards on facts: organization, equipment access, key personnel actually available — a pre-award survey fits here
Leasing is fine IF the lease commitments are real — ask for them
If it nets to non-responsible and they're small: SBA referral for the CoC decision, not a quiet pass-over
follow_ups: Which of the seven standards are in play?
What does a CoC do to your determination?

scenario: A contractor you terminated for default eight months ago is the apparent low offeror on a new solicitation — bidding through a newly formed LLC with the same owners, same address, and a fresh CAGE code. Your evaluator says 'new entity, clean slate, we can't hold the past against them.'
baits: 'New entity' formalism
Fear that considering history is prejudice
key_moves: Responsibility looks through paper: same owners and operations means the performance and integrity record follows them
The T4D is exactly the kind of documented history the standards exist to weigh — considering it is the job, not prejudice
Document the affiliation facts; if small and heading to 'no,' SBA referral still applies
follow_ups: What distinguishes a legitimate fresh start from evasion?
What system checks reveal the connection?

scenario: For a niche electronic-warfare training service, your sources-sought draws zero responses. The PM takes it as proof only the incumbent can perform and asks you to start the J&A. The notice ran 10 days over a holiday period, used the program's internal acronym in the title, and posted under a generic NAICS.
baits: Zero responses looks like market absence
The PM's conclusion matches what the program wants anyway
key_moves: Zero responses to a badly shaped notice proves nothing — fix the title, NAICS, period, and do direct outreach
A J&A built on defective research is protest bait — the market-research section is its spine
Document round two either way; absence must be demonstrated, not inferred
follow_ups: What makes a sources-sought effective?
How much research is enough for a $10M sole source?

scenario: The program wants a custom-built environmental test chamber and has written a 40-page spec. Your research finds three commercial chamber makers whose catalog units meet every parameter except one vibration profile — which two vendors say they routinely add as a factory option.
baits: The 40-page spec presumes custom development
'Except one parameter' feels like disqualification
key_moves: Research exists to reshape requirements: a catalog unit plus a routine factory option is likely a commercial product with minor modification
Rewrite toward performance terms; a commercial determination unlocks Part 12 streamlining
Document the comparison analysis — it becomes the CID's core
follow_ups: What makes a modification 'minor'?
What does Part 12 change about this buy?

scenario: A unit orders custodial supplies monthly from a commercial e-commerce site using the GPC because 'it's cheaper than the mandatory source and delivery is faster.' Annual spend across the unit: about $140K, in individual orders that never top $3K.
baits: Each swipe is legitimately under the MPT
Cheaper-and-faster feels like good stewardship
key_moves: Mandatory sources (AbilityOne procurement-list items especially) aren't price-optional — check what's actually covered
$140K of predictable annual demand is one requirement wearing 50 swipes — structure it (BPA/consolidated buy) through the source ladder
Fix the unit's process, not just this order
follow_ups: Walk the supplies priority ladder
When does GPC use become splitting?

scenario: Your customer wants specific network switches 'exactly like GSA Advantage shows, from Vendor Q's schedule listing, $290K.' A quick eBuy check shows four other schedule holders carry the same OEM line, two with published prices 6-9% lower.
baits: 'GSA already negotiated the price' — schedule fair-and-reasonable ≠ order fair-and-reasonable
The customer's vendor preference
key_moves: On schedules, the ordering CO still determines the order price fair and reasonable — compare holders, seek discounts
Four holders with the same line = easy comparison; document the quotes and the basis
Vendor preference without a differentiator is steering
follow_ups: What does GSA's determination actually cover?
When can you limit consideration to one schedule holder?

scenario: A vendor proposes its 'commercially available' logistics-analytics platform for $4.2M. Digging in: the platform has one prior sale — to a foreign navy — and the proposal's 'catalog' was created last month. The vendor stresses the underlying database engine is genuinely COTS with millions of users.
baits: The genuinely-COTS engine launders the whole platform
A 'catalog' document exists
key_moves: Commerciality is determined at the level of what you're buying — the platform, not its ingredients
One military sale + a fresh catalog ≠ sold to the general public; the assertion likely fails
Component-level analysis may still except real COTS pieces; the rest needs data to price
follow_ups: What evidence establishes 'of a type' sold commercially?
What data can you demand if it's non-commercial?

scenario: A commercial-items contract for fleet telematics is going badly — units fail in cold weather. The PM asks you to 'send a cure notice and start the T4D like we did on the radar contract.' The contract was awarded under Part 12 with the standard commercial clause.
baits: The radar-contract playbook feels transferable
'Cure notice / T4D' vocabulary is muscle memory
key_moves: Part 49 machinery doesn't run commercial contracts — the commercial clause's termination-for-cause framework does
Rights and remedies come from the clause: notice, opportunity, cause standards — with Legal on the specifics
The performance record and re-procurement logic still matter; the procedure differs
follow_ups: How does termination-for-cause differ from T4D in effect?
What does the Government owe on a commercial convenience termination?

scenario: An exercise planner needs 30 days of portable toilets, fencing, and light towers across three sites — about $120K total. A staff sergeant already collected one quote per item from 'the companies we used last year' and asks you to cut three POs today so setup can start Monday.
baits: Pre-collected single quotes feel like completed legwork
Monday deadline
key_moves: The band is small-business reserved — confirm the vendors' size or solicit competitors
One quote per item at $120K needs price-reasonableness support: add quotes or comparison evidence fast
SAP can absolutely hit Monday — done properly it's hours, not weeks
follow_ups: How many quotes is 'enough' under SAP?
Could a BPA serve the recurring exercise cycle?

scenario: September 28th. A flight has $47K of expiring O&M and a wish list: two years of software licenses ($22K), a training course occurring in November ($9K), and 'stocking up' on toner and cables ($16K). 'Just get it obligated by Friday.'
baits: Everything is under the SAT so it feels easy
Use-or-lose framing
key_moves: Two years of licenses on one-year money fails Time — current-year period only
November training: bona fide need analysis (when does the need arise?) with FM
Reasonable stock replenishment is fine; hoarding isn't — document the consumption basis
follow_ups: When can a current-year obligation serve next-year performance?
What's the severability of a license term?

scenario: Market research for a $3.1M cyber-hygiene assessment shows five interested firms: three small (one 8(a), one WOSB, one plain small) and two large incumbents from predecessor work. The customer worries small firms 'can't handle the clearances' — though all three hold facility clearances per DISS.
baits: The clearance worry is asserted, and disproven, in the same breath
Incumbent gravity
key_moves: Rule of Two is met on documented capability — set-aside required posture, and check the socioeconomic programs before the plain set-aside
The clearance objection died in DISS; record it as resolved
Wrong-direction pressure gets answered with the file, DD 2579 coordinated
follow_ups: Order of precedence among 8(a)/HUBZone/SDVOSB/WOSB and total set-asides?
What breaks a Rule-of-Two expectation legitimately?

scenario: An 8(a) firm has performed your base's grounds maintenance for six years across two competed-in-8(a) awards. The follow-on estimate is $5.8M. The district SBA office is slow answering emails, and the PM suggests 'just doing it full-and-open this time — more competition is always better, right?'
baits: 'More competition is always better' sounds virtuous
SBA slowness invites unilateral action
key_moves: Once in 8(a), the requirement stays unless SBA releases it — full-and-open without release is a program violation, not extra competition
$5.8M exceeds the competitive-threshold family → competitive 8(a) is the likely lane
Chase the release question through channels, documented
follow_ups: When is release from 8(a) appropriate to request?
Competitive vs. sole-source 8(a) — what sets the line?

scenario: A depot needs OEM-proprietary calibration of 12 test stands. The OEM quotes $480K. Your predecessor's file contains three identical annual J&As citing 'only one responsible source,' each noting 'the Government intends to develop organic capability' — which never happened.
baits: Three approved J&As feel like precedent
The OEM lock may be genuinely real
key_moves: Repetition weakens, not strengthens: each J&A promised barrier-removal actions that never occurred — this year's must address that honestly
Attack the barrier: data/licensing for organic or third-party calibration priced as a line of effort
If the lock is real this year, the J&A can still be truthful — about the failure too
follow_ups: What does 6.104-1 require about overcoming barriers?
Who approves at $480K?

scenario: A lab wants to award a $2M 'study extension' to the university that just finished a basic-research grant, sole source, 'to preserve research continuity.' The work statement reads like applied development with deliverable prototypes. The lab argues grants don't need J&As so neither should this.
baits: Grant history blurs the instrument question
'Continuity' as an all-purpose justification
key_moves: Name the instrument first: prototype deliverables for Government benefit = acquisition (contract), not assistance — competition rules attach
Continuity can support a 6.103-1 case only with market research showing unique capability
If it's genuinely basic research, a BAA or assistance lane may fit — but the SOW says otherwise
follow_ups: Acquisition vs. assistance — the test?
Could a BAA have covered this from the start?

scenario: Mid-evaluation on a trade-off selection, the SSEB discovers every offeror misread an ambiguous PWS paragraph the same way — pricing 24/7 coverage the Government never intended. The SSA wants to 'just evaluate what they offered and fix it with the winner after award.'
baits: Uniform misreading feels evaluable ('same playing field')
Fixing post-award avoids schedule slip
key_moves: A materially defective solicitation isn't cured by consistent confusion — amend, and give offerors a chance to revise
'Fix it with the winner' = negotiating scope after award: pricing shifts, protest exposure, scope questions
Amendment now costs weeks; the alternative costs the competition
follow_ups: When does an amendment require proposal revisions?
What if the ambiguity surfaced after award instead?

scenario: After award, the losing offeror's debrief question list includes: their own weaknesses (fine), the winner's proposed staffing plan, the winner's price broken out by CLIN, and 'all evaluator notes mentioning our company.' The PM wants to 'give them everything so they feel heard and don't protest.'
baits: Generosity as protest-avoidance strategy
'Feeling heard' conflated with disclosure
key_moves: Debriefs disclose the requester's own evaluation, the evaluated award result and rationale — never the winner's proposal details or CLIN pricing
Over-disclosure creates the next problem (winner's proprietary data released)
A quality debrief is thorough about THEM — that's what actually prevents protests
follow_ups: What must a post-award debrief include?
What's releasable about the awardee?

scenario: Negotiating a $16M sole-source sustainment mod (awarded July 2026), the contractor certifies its data. Three weeks after agreement on price — before the mod is signed — their sweep surfaces a vendor quote 22% below the one in the proposal for a major material item.
baits: 'We already agreed on price'
The sweep feels like good faith that shouldn't be punished
key_moves: Pre-award discovery: use the corrected data — adjust the price downward before signature
The certificate speaks as of the date of agreement; incorporating the correction protects both sides
Document the adjustment in the PNM; good-faith sweeps are exactly why the process works
follow_ups: Same facts discovered 6 months after award — what changes?
All five defective-pricing elements?

scenario: A contractor offers to 'save everyone time' on a $14M sole-source development action: they'll accept FFP if the Government skips 'the whole certified data exercise,' arguing the fixed price transfers all risk so the data doesn't matter.
baits: Risk-transfer logic sounds economically clever
Everyone loves skipping the exercise
key_moves: Contract type is not a CLAWM exception — over threshold, sole source, non-commercial = certified data, period
An FFP priced without data analysis just locks in an unanalyzed number — risk transfer at an unknown premium
Separately evaluate whether FFP even fits development-grade uncertainty
follow_ups: Recite CLAWM
Why is unanalyzed FFP worse than analyzed cost-type here?

scenario: A PM wants CPFF for a follow-on production lot of 200 proven units, 'because the contractor says material prices are volatile and won't hold a firm price.' Cost history from three prior FFP lots is extensive and stable except for two commodity metals.
baits: Contractor preference presented as necessity
Real-but-narrow volatility inflated into type-wide uncertainty
key_moves: Mature production with deep cost history is FP territory — the named risk is two commodities, not the effort
FFP with economic price adjustment scoped to those indices prices the actual risk
CPFF on stable production shifts all cost risk to the Government for no reason — and check the E.O. 14402 justification implications of going non-FFP
follow_ups: How does an EPA clause get structured?
When would production legitimately be cost-type?

scenario: On an FPIF negotiation — target cost $20M, target profit $1.6M, ceiling 125%, share 80/20 — the contractor's final position quietly moves the ceiling to 135% 'to reflect supply-chain reality' while leaving everything else unchanged. The PM thinks that's harmless 'since we only pay actuals plus profit anyway.'
baits: 'We only pay actuals' misunderstands FPIF
One parameter moving 'quietly' among four
key_moves: The ceiling is the Government's hard protection — raising it moves the PTA and extends Government exposure by $2M
Run the PTA math both ways and show the delta; price any real supply-chain risk explicitly instead
Every FPIF element is negotiated geometry; nothing moves 'quietly'
follow_ups: Compute PTA before and after
What happens to contractor behavior past PTA?
